title: Rembrandt and the Flemish School
subject: art
description: **Rembrandt van Rijn** was the great painter of the Dutch Golden Age. Self-portraits, biblical scenes, and *The Night Watch*: he painted the human soul.

hero.hook: From the glory of Amsterdam to ruin: the painter who turned shadow into a language of the soul.

blocks.text: **Rembrandt van Rijn** (1606-1669) was the master of the 17th-century Dutch school. During the [[Dutch Golden Age]], the Netherlands became a commercial power and a home for free thinking.
His self-portraits, his biblical scenes, and his famous *Night Watch* turned chiaroscuro into an emotional language. He put human beings, splendid or worn out, at the center of everything.

In the 17th century, the **United Provinces** dominated world trade. In the rest of Europe, the Church and kings ordered the art. In Holland, the market was driven by a Protestant middle class that wanted paintings for the home, not frescoes for a church.

That created room for new genres: landscape, still life, scenes of daily life. **Vermeer** and [[Hals]] made their names in them. Rembrandt settled in Amsterdam in **1631** and became the most sought-after portraitist in the city.
After the bankruptcy, his son Titus and his partner Hendrickje set up an art dealership with Rembrandt as its official employee, to keep his new canvases away from creditors.
But he lived far beyond his means. In **1656**, [[personal bankruptcy]] hit him. House, furniture, and collections went to auction. Even then he refused to soften his style to suit fashion.

Rembrandt reinvented the [[chiaroscuro]] he inherited from [[Caravaggio]]. In his work, light does not strike only for effect: it seems to filter out from inside the figures. The eye settles on faces and hands.

blocks.caption: The Night Watch: a militia on the move, not a frozen row of men

blocks.text: His other signature was **impasto**, paint laid on so thick that it stands up off the canvas. In an age that wanted smooth surfaces, he dared to show the material. People joked that some of his portraits could be lifted by the nose. He was after the true, not the ideally beautiful.
Chemical analysis has found plumbonacrite in his impasto: a rare lead compound that helped his thick layers dry faster.

sections.title: The Night Watch: a portrait that moves

blocks.text: In **1642**, Rembrandt delivered *The Company of Captain Frans Banning Cocq*, known as **The Night Watch**. It was a commission for the [[Kloveniersdoelen]], the headquarters of an Amsterdam civic guard. Normally the guardsmen posed in a line, each clearly visible because each had paid.

Rembrandt showed them in motion, marching out of their headquarters. Chiaroscuro ranks the figures: some slip into shadow. Legend says the furious guardsmen brought about his downfall. In fact the painting was admired, even if it puzzled people.
The title *The Night Watch* is a mistake: the scene takes place in daylight. Centuries of dirty varnish darkened the canvas so much that people took it for a night patrol.
In the 18th century, to fit it into the Town Hall, all four sides were cut down. Some figures vanished. The original composition was far more spacious.

Rembrandt painted roughly **80 to 90 self-portraits** over nearly forty years. Young, he showed himself arrogant, wrapped in furs and jewels. After the ruin and the deaths in his family, the tone changed: no charm left, only a raw honesty about growing old.

blocks.text: He died in **1669** and was buried without ceremony, yet his influence runs from Goya to [[Francis Bacon]]. He remains the painter who turned pigment into inner light.
Rembrandt magnified the human interior through chiaroscuro and thick paint. From the glory of Amsterdam to ruin, his self-portraits remain a unique diary of a life.
